results.content: # Gender Variation in Mix-Gender Conversations in the Semi-institutional Discourse: The Case of Talk Show. In this paper, gender-related variations in the semi-institutional discourse are examined. We investigate the cross-gender conversation in the talk show *Behind the Headline with Wentao*, a corpus of around 88,000 words of Mandarin Chinese conversation and identify gender variation between female and male guests. We explore the turn-taking features and characteristic terms that set the gender categories apart. The results also suggest that male and female speakers tend to use more gendered terms when the conversational topics involved people and relationships. # Janet Holmes (linguist). * Edit&action=edit "Edit this page [e]"). * Edit&action=edit "Edit this page [e]"). **Janet Holmes** ONZM (born 17 May 1947) is a New Zealand sociolinguist. Her research interests include language and gender, language in the workplace, and New Zealand English. After obtaining an MPhil at the University of Leeds, Holmes moved to Victoria University of Wellington in New Zealand, later becoming a naturalised New Zealander in 1975. She is now an Emeritus Professor of Linguistics at Victoria University of Wellington, New Zealand. In 1996, she established the Wellington Language in the Workplace (LWP) project, which is an ongoing study of communication formats occurring in the workplace, which examines “small talk, humour, management strategies, directives, and leadership in a wide range of New Zealand workplaces”. Holmes has been featured on the media, such as the Radio New Zealand and newspapers. In recognition of Holmes' contributions to the field of Sociolinguistics, *Linguist at Work: Festschrift for Janet Holmes* brings together works by Holmes's colleagues, students, collaborators, and friends which present new ideas and analysis within the field. In the 2016 New Year Honours "2016 New Year Honours (New Zealand)"), Holmes was appointed an Officer of the New Zealand Order of Merit for services to linguistics. results.title: On the Lexical Hypothesis. The Limits of Language in Personality… | by Carl Georg Solberg, PhD | Medium
results.content: ## The Limits of Language in Personality Psychology. A widely accepted idea in this field is the “lexical hypothesis” — the notion that the most important differences between people become encoded as words in language. But in a piercing analysis, psychologist Patrick Mollaret argues that the lexical hypothesis rests on shaky assumptions.¹ He contends that equating language with personality overlooks the incredible complexity of human behavior and psychology. While language may encode differences between people, Mollaret contends the lexical hypothesis erroneously equates difference with disposition. Just because people vary along some dimension does not mean those variations reflect ingrained psychological traits. Yet wealth itself does not constitute a personality trait, as earning differences depend on numerous complex external and systemic factors beyond just individual psychology. Similarly, Mollaret argues that the lexical hypothesis unfoundedly extrapolates disposition from variability. Personality inventories developed through the lexical approach cannot verify hypothesized traits within individuals. An even more troubling pitfall lies in the lexical hypothesis’s categorization of messy vocabulary into ostensibly neat psychological structures. Yet the lexical hypothesis flattens this nuance by tying words to specific traits. For instance, Mollaret argues the common demarcation between fleeting “state” words and enduring “trait” words reflects particular cultural ideologies, not innate linguistic boundaries. Overall, the lexical hypothesis risks reifying complex social semantics into seemingly formal psychological categories. **Beyond Words: Exploring Personality Through Culture**. Rather than definitive traits, Mollaret proposes personality words gain meaning through their usage in broader “forms of life” — the social and cultural practices that contextualize language. Reconceptualizing personality language as contingently shaped by cultural factors rather than universally reflecting traits opens promising research avenues. Psychologists could illuminate how distinct settings imbue words with particular connotations — escaping the narrow lexical framework to embrace the rich complexity of social context influencing personality semantics. It highlights the need to untangle the intricate linkages between vocabulary, culture and human personality without relying on overly simplistic lexical categories. His critique enriches personality psychology by unveiling the diverse meanings words adopt through nuanced cultural shaping rather than merely labeling hypothesized inner essences.
